title: One sea, not both
standfirst: The easiest country in the region to travel well, and the easiest to travel badly.

blocks.heading: The two coasts are never in season together
paras: Thailand's Andaman and Gulf coasts run on opposite monsoons. An itinerary that visits both in one trip will be wet on one of them.
We pick the sea that suits the month and stay with it, then use the north for contrast rather than a second beach.

blocks.heading: North for the contrast
blocks.caption: Jungle camps and hill country, a short flight from the coast.
paras: The north is cooler, greener and entirely different in texture from the islands, and most itineraries treat it as an afterthought.
Four nights in the hills before the sea makes the beach feel earned rather than default.

blocks.heading: A boat, not a tour
blocks.caption: A boat held for the stay rather than booked by the day.
paras: The limestone bays are magnificent at seven in the morning and unbearable by eleven, when the day boats arrive.
We hold a boat and a skipper for the whole stay, which buys the early hours and the empty anchorages.

blocks.heading: Questions members ask
blocks.intro: The ones that come up nearly every time.

a: November to March for the Andaman side; the Gulf islands run later and hold up well into September.

items.q: Bangkok at the start or the end?
a: The start, always. A city at the end of a beach week undoes the beach week.
For four or more people, a villa with staff is almost always better value and considerably more private than connecting suites.

blocks.heading: We are ready when you are
paras: Every itinerary starts with a conversation about what you actually want from the days, and works backwards to houses, guides and timing from there.
